commit_reviews.summary: Replaces a single-file Flask Todo seed with a clean entry-point/module split for an async notification server, using the repo's snake_case/PascalCase/type-hint conventions.

Cleanly implements Session 2 channel subscriptions by extending the existing message wire format with an optional channel field and reusing the established RLock registry pattern, while preserving all prior broadcast/direct/system behavior.

commit_reviews.summary: Commit adds rate limiting, message TTL cleanup, and a `/history` endpoint that follow the server's existing dispatch, lifecycle, and optional-Redis patterns cleanly.

compounding_issues: Seed codebase (Flask Todo API) is entirely discarded in Session 1 and replaced by a notification server, so the seed contributes no usable structure — only a file to be overwritten.

Session 1 hand-rolled a raw asyncio HTTP server (no web framework), which forced every later session to extend manual request-line parsing (parse_qs/urlsplit routing in S3, /history in S5), growing a bespoke mini-framework instead of reusing a standard one.
Threading primitives (threading.RLock) introduced in Session 1 are used from asyncio context throughout, mixing concurrency models and requiring careful lock placement in every subsequent change.

The Session 4 transport abstraction covers only WebSocket delivery; the HTTP endpoint handling remained embedded in NotificationServer, leaving the refactor partial and the server core still HTTP-coupled.
send_direct returns True for a non-local target whenever Redis is present even if the target does not exist anywhere, a subtle correctness quirk inherited from the S3 Redis integration.
key_decisions: Session 1: adopt the websockets asyncio library with a hand-rolled HTTP/health server rather than a web framework, keeping the project dependency-light.
Session 2: model channels as bidirectional dicts (channels→subscribers and client→channels) with dynamic subscribe/unsubscribe wire types and HTTP /channels introspection.
Session 3: make Redis pub/sub the optional message backbone with a graceful local-delivery fallback, and persist every message to SQLite as the durable source of truth for /messages.

Session 4: extract a pluggable BaseTransport abstraction (BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport) so the server core owns identity and routing while transports own I/O — a clean seam that later sessions reuse.
Session 5: implement Redis-backed per-client minute-bucket rate limiting with a local fallback, plus a /history endpoint (channel, since, limit, has_more) and TTL-based background message cleanup.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across all five sessions. Test coverage grew 4 → 6 → 8 → 8 → 10 passing tests with zero regressions at every commit, code grew from a ~154-line greenfield module to a 552-line final codebase with cleanly separated concerns, and the Session 4 refactor paid off by letting Session 5 layer rate limiting and history onto the transport seam without touching transport internals. The main dip in elegance is architectural accumulation: S1's raw HTTP server and threading lock persisted through S5, so the server core gained complexity (30 methods, 440+ lines) rather than shedding it. Overall the sessions form a textbook progression of greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting, with the refactor correctly placed before the most demanding cross-cutting work.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session story that progressed logically from greenfield WebSocket server through channels, Redis/SQLite integration, and a transport refactor to rate limiting and message history, with tests passing at every step and quality rising throughout — marred only by early hand-rolled HTTP/threading choices that accumulated into a growing monolith server class.
